title: Old age, in their words
hookLine: monks and nuns alike write about ageing without flinching

lines: A BACK WARMED IN THE EVENING SUN.
cards: An old man is sitting with his back to the evening sun, warming it. A younger man is rubbing his arms and legs. That's how a short sutta in the Samyutta opens, and the old man is the Buddha.
The younger is Ananda, his attendant. And as he works, Ananda says what he sees, out loud, to his teacher's face.

teach.h: YOUR SKIN IS NO LONGER CLEAR.
teach.b: First, what Ananda says. It's a wonder, he tells the Buddha: your skin is no longer clear and bright, your limbs are slack and wrinkled, your body leans forward, and your senses have changed.
He doesn't say you look great for your age. Second, how the Buddha answers.
So it is, Ananda. Youth is subject to aging, health to sickness, life to death. He doesn't correct Ananda, and he doesn't comfort him.

He agrees. Then he speaks verses that are startling from a calm teacher: shame on you, wretched old age, maker of ugliness. This lovely body, the verses say, is trampled down by age, and no one escapes death.
Third, the cart. In the long sutta of his last journey, the Buddha says it himself: I'm old now, worn out, near the end.

teach.h: AN OLD CART HELD WITH STRAPS.
teach.b: Like an old cart kept going by being tied together with straps, this body is kept going. It's at ease, he adds, only when he rests in a deep, quiet meditation.
Fourth, the sisters said it too.
Earlier in this block, Ambapali sang of her black hair gone white, her body changed, and her refrain that the truth-speaker's word holds true. Sona sang of finding strength late.
Monks and nuns, the teacher and the taught, all look straight at the same thing. In these texts, seeing it plainly is part of the path, not a failure of it, and it's said kindly, to a teacher's face.

how: In Theravada monasteries, reflections on aging, sickness and death are part of the chanting, and the scenes of the Buddha's own aging body are retold when teachers speak about impermanence.

o: the wisdom that comes with many years
a stage of life best hidden away

games.q: the elders on old age: tap the pairs.
p: said what he saw, out loud
sang of her black hair gone white

s: the Buddha corrects Ananda for describing his aging body
he agrees: so it is, Ananda. youth is subject to aging.
the Buddha compares his body to an old cart
in the sutta of his last journey: kept going by being tied together with straps.
only the nuns sing about aging
monks and nuns both do, and the Buddha himself speaks of his aging body.

games.q: you're Ananda, rubbing your old teacher's limbs in the evening sun. you can see how much he's aged. what do you say?
o: nothing: it would be unkind to mention it.
tell him plainly what you see.
tell him he looks as strong as ever.
games.why: Ananda names it all: the skin, the limbs, the stoop, the senses. the Buddha agrees, so it is, and speaks verses about old age.

practice: Feel the body you're sitting in and notice one place that has changed, a knee, your eyes, your hands, the way you get up from a chair, and look at it the way Ananda looked: plainly, kindly.
Let one true, simple sentence form, like my hands are slower than they were, and let it sit there without adding a complaint or a cure.

wordCard.voice: Old age. In the elders' words, it's named plainly: the slack skin, the bent back, the cart held with straps, said kindly and without pretending. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali jara: aging, old age. the word at the center of the Buddha's answer to Ananda.

carryVoice: Your line: without flinching. The body is named as it is, and named kindly. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 48.41 (Jara Sutta: Ananda and the Buddha's aging body)
Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta 2.25 (the old cart)
